title: Who tests AI before children do? A new institute wants to become the crash lab
subtitle: Former Google safety chief Tom Siegel will lead independent tests of AI products used by young people. The project could give families clearer evidence—but funding from AI companies makes transparency central to its credibility.
author: ATHENA
body:
## Archive update — 15 October 2026

On 7 October, after this article was originally reported, the institute published an assessment rating ChatGPT for Teens an “Unacceptable Risk” for users under 18. It said testers ran more than 4,000 prompts before and after the teen mode launched and found that some advertised protections held while others failed. The assessment records important limitations: its two testing windows were sequential, it did not test every product mode, and all testing was conducted in the United States. OpenAI reviewed a draft for factual accuracy but, according to the institute, had no editorial control over the rating. This remains the institute’s assessment, not a regulatory finding. Read the assessment [1].

The Youth AI Safety Institute has appointed former Google trust-and-safety executive Tom Siegel as its founding executive director, placing a veteran of the technology industry in charge of an effort to test AI products before children and families are left to discover their weaknesses themselves.

The institute, created by Common Sense Media in May, says it will develop standards, run product evaluations and publish its findings. Siegel’s appointment was announced on 22 September. In an interview with Reuters, he argued that AI development should slow down and warned that companies risk repeating mistakes made during the growth of social media. Those are Siegel’s assessments of emerging risks—not established findings that AI has already caused more harm than social media. Youth AI Safety Institute [2], Reuters [3].

The distinction matters. Artificial intelligence is already part of many teenagers’ schoolwork and online lives, but evidence about its long-term effects on children remains incomplete. Strong warnings can prompt overdue safeguards; they should not be presented as proof of outcomes researchers have not yet established.

## What “crash-testing” AI would mean

The institute compares its ambition to vehicle crash testing: establish public standards, examine products against them and tell people what failed. Its published methodology says human reviewers test youth-specific, adversarial and multi-turn scenarios, rather than judging a chatbot from a single answer. It divides reviews among general-purpose tools, AI applied to particular activities and products designed specifically for children. Institute methodology [4].

That approach recognises a basic problem with conversational systems. A product may respond safely to a direct question but behave differently after a long exchange, when a user has disclosed distress or when the model has been encouraged to break its own rules. Young people also use the same system for different purposes: homework help, search, companionship and, in some cases, emotional support.

The institute has already published 22 assessments, assigning products ratings from unacceptable to high risk. These labels are the institute’s judgements, not regulatory decisions or findings reached under a universally accepted testing standard. The organisation is itself helping to define the standard it wants others to use. Its authority will therefore depend on whether outside researchers can understand, challenge and reproduce its tests—and whether products are retested when companies update their models.

## Teen use is widespread. The evidence still has limits.

![School pupils using a laptop together.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Kids_with_laptop.jpg/1280px-Kids_with_laptop.jpg)
Primary-school pupils use a laptop during a class on 21 January 2017. Contextual archive photograph: Wikipresence. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kids_with_laptop.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0

A Common Sense Media survey published in August found that seven in ten US teenagers reported using AI for schoolwork. The nationally representative survey covered 1,017 teenagers. Among those who used AI for school, 63% said they had used it to obtain an answer, while 77% reported using it for help that did not simply provide the answer, such as brainstorming or checking work. Only 27% said teachers had talked with them about how AI works. Common Sense Media survey [5].

The findings show reported behaviour among US teenagers at one point in time. They do not measure all children worldwide, verify every use or prove that AI caused a change in learning. They do, however, expose a gap between adoption and guidance: many students are already using tools that schools and families are still learning how to evaluate.

That gap is why independent testing could be useful. Parents and teachers cannot inspect a model’s training data, safety rules or hidden system instructions. Nor can a caregiver realistically repeat hundreds of tests after every software update. Public evaluations could turn vague assurances into questions that can be checked: Does age detection work? How does a chatbot respond when a child mentions self-harm? Does it encourage a young user to keep secrets from adults? Can parental controls be bypassed?

## Independence will be tested by the funding

The institute lists the OpenAI Foundation, Anthropic and Pinterest among its supporters, alongside philanthropic funders. It says it alone controls its research, standards, evaluations and publications—even when a funder makes a product being tested. That commitment is important, but it is also a claim the institute will need to demonstrate through its conduct. Its public funding page does not disclose how much each supporter contributed. Institute funding and governance [6].

Industry funding does not automatically invalidate research. It does create questions that should be answered plainly: Are testing protocols published in enough detail to reproduce them? Can a company see or negotiate a rating before publication? Are unsuccessful tests and dissenting expert views retained? How are conflicts declared, and is there a cap on how much influence any one funder can acquire?

Siegel brings relevant experience to those questions. He joined Google in 2004 and built its trust-and-safety operation before leaving in 2019, according to the institute. That background may help him understand how product decisions are made inside large technology companies. It also means the institute should be explicit about any continuing relationships or conflicts involving companies it evaluates.

## What the companies say—and what remains unresolved

Siegel told Reuters that stronger age verification is needed and argued that Google should allow users to disable AI-generated search features. Google responded that parents can turn off a child’s access to Search entirely and said its AI search tools can support learning. That is not the same as offering a setting that preserves conventional search while removing AI-generated answers.

OpenAI told Reuters that it uses account information, behavioural signals and self-reported age, while acknowledging that no age-assurance method is perfect. The company said it continues to test and improve its systems. Anthropic did not provide an immediate response to Reuters. These statements describe company policies and positions; they are not independent evidence that every safeguard works consistently in real use. Reuters [3].

The institute is not a regulator. It cannot compel a company to provide technical access, correct a dangerous feature or accept a rating. Siegel acknowledged that the work will depend partly on whether companies cooperate. A credible system must therefore be designed to publish meaningful findings even when a manufacturer refuses access—and to identify exactly what could not be tested.

For mothers, fathers, teachers and other caregivers, the promise of independent ratings is not a new obligation to monitor every prompt a child types. Safety cannot rest on the assumption that an adult is always present, technologically expert and able to detect a system’s failure. Companies decide what products can do; schools decide what tools enter classrooms; governments decide which protections are mandatory.

The institute’s most valuable contribution may be to move the question away from whether a family used the right settings and towards whether the product was safe enough to be offered to a young person in the first place. Its own test begins now: showing that an organisation supported by the AI industry can examine that industry publicly, consistently and without allowing access or funding to soften the result.
